description: What Node.js is and how to run JavaScript outside the browser.

screens.body:
Node.js is a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser. Inside a browser tab, JavaScript can only touch the web page — Node sets it free.

With Node, your JavaScript can read files, talk to databases, and run web servers. Same language you already know, brand-new superpowers.

It's built on Chrome's V8 engine — the thing that already made browser JavaScript fast.

options: Run anywhere — your computer, a server, not just a browser tab
Only run inside a browser tab
check.question: What does Node.js let JavaScript do?

screens.heading: What is Node, anyway?
screens.keyPoint: Node = JavaScript that escaped the browser.

screens.body:
Node usually comes bundled with npm (its package manager — next topic). Two commands tell you if you're set up.

node -v prints the Node version. npm -v prints the npm version. If both print version numbers, you're good to go.

No output or a "not recognized" error? Grab the installer from nodejs.org and run it again.

options: Node is installed — that's its version number
JavaScript is broken on your machine
check.question: You type node -v and see v22.14.0. What does that mean?

screens.heading: Check your install
screens.keyPoint: node -v and npm -v: version numbers = you're ready.

screens.body:
Running JavaScript with Node is delightfully boring: save your code in a .js file, then point Node at it.

No HTML file, no browser, no build step. Just a file and a command.

console.log works exactly like it does in the browser — it prints to the terminal instead of the dev console.

check.question: How do you run a file called server.js with Node?

screens.heading: Your first script
screens.keyPoint: Save code in app.js, run it with node app.js.

screens.body:
Type node with nothing after it and you land in the REPL — an interactive prompt for trying out JavaScript line by line.

REPL stands for Read, Eval, Print, Loop: it reads what you type, runs it, prints the result, and waits for more.

It's perfect for quick experiments. Type .exit (or press Ctrl+C twice) to leave.

options: Open the Node REPL by typing node
Create a whole new project folder
check.question: What's the fastest way to test a one-line JavaScript idea?

screens.heading: The REPL playground
screens.keyPoint: node alone = instant playground for one-line ideas.

screens.body:
Two globals you'll meet constantly. console is the familiar one — console.log prints to the terminal.

process describes the program that's currently running. process.version gives the Node version, process.platform tells you the operating system.

process.argv is a bonus: it's the list of command-line arguments your script was started with. (You'll play with it in the exercises.)

options: Which operating system Node is running on
How many files are currently open
check.question: What does process.platform tell you?

screens.heading: console and process
screens.keyPoint: process = facts about the running program.

screens.body:
Node ships with built-in modules — ready-made tools for files, paths, the network, and more. No installing anything.

The file-system module is called fs. Requiring it gives you functions like readdirSync, which lists the files in a folder.

(You'll learn require properly in the Modules topic — for now, just know the toolbox is already there.)

check.question: You want to list the files in a folder from Node. Which built-in module helps?

screens.heading: Built-in superpowers
screens.keyPoint: fs, path, http and friends come free with Node.

screens.body:
Node runs your code on a single thread — one waiter serving a whole restaurant. So how does it handle thousands of requests?

It never blocks. When Node starts reading a file or waiting on a database, it doesn't freeze — it takes other orders in the meantime and comes back when the food (data) is ready.

This juggling act is called the event loop. The takeaway: slow tasks don't freeze your app, they just get handled in the background.

options: It works non-blocking — other tasks continue while it waits
It skips files that are too big
check.question: Why doesn't Node freeze while reading a big file?

screens.heading: One waiter, many tables
screens.keyPoint: Node doesn't freeze while waiting — it juggles.
